title: Juniper and the Lantern
premise: In 1913, Hazel Villalobos drives for suffragist organizer Edith Marchmont and has quietly read every letter she delivers, learning that silence can be a form of protection. When one sealed letter reveals the Marchmont family is being framed in an arson plot by political rivals, Hazel must choose between her invisibility and the only people who ever made her feel she belonged. She smuggles the evidence through three checkpoints to reach the ship carrying the family's lawyer before dawn, exposing the conspiracy at great personal cost. In the end, Hazel steps out of the shadows—testifying under her own name—and finds that belonging was never something she could earn by disappearing.
about_author: Rafael Galloway is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing letters from the American suffrage movement. This is their second novel exploring the quiet lives behind historical movements.

chapters.title: The Weight of Sealed Things
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. We meet Hazel on a rain-slicked Boston morning as she drives Edith Marchmont to a rally, establishing her ritual of reading letters by lamplight and her careful choreography of invisibility. Emotional beat: the comfort and loneliness of being trusted but unseen.

chapters.title: What the Mistress Doesn't Say
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. A letter from Edith's estranged brother arrives; Hazel reads it and senses coded warnings about 'the warehouse on the tide.' She begins mapping the household's silences—who avoids whom at dinner, which doors stay locked. Emotional beat: unease sharpening into suspicion.

chapters.title: Ash on the Water
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. The harbor warehouse burns; no one dies, but the papers inside would have cleared the Marchmont name in an old scandal. Edith suspects her brother's business partners and asks Hazel, for the first time, to do something outside her role. Emotional beat: fear disguised as composure.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel learns the evidence—a ledger naming the plotters—is hidden in a sealed letter addressed to the family's lawyer aboard the SS Corvina, sailing on the morning tide. Police loyal to the conspirators man three checkpoints between the house and the pier. Emotional beat: resolve crystallizing into a plan.

chapters.title: The Lantern in the Hall
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, with a flashback to her first year of service. She retrieves the letter from Edith's writing desk and confronts why she reads what she shouldn't: ten years ago a letter she failed to read cost someone her life. Emotional beat: guilt transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: A Man Who Counts Doors
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. At the first checkpoint, a detective named Brogan—who has been watching the house for weeks—questions her at length. She survives on the very skill of seeming unremarkable, but realizes he recognized her eyes, not her face. Emotional beat: terror held beneath stillness.

chapters.title: The Second Gate
chapters.summary: Alternating Hazel and Edith POVs. At the customs shed, the letter is nearly opened when Edith arrives unannounced, claiming Hazel carries her private correspondence and invoking a scandalous threat of her own. Mother-figure and driver stand together for the first time as equals. Emotional beat: love against duty, both women choosing each other over safety.

chapters.title: Brogan's Choice
chapters.summary: Brogan's POV. At the final checkpoint on the pier, Brogan corners Hazel alone—he knows what the letter contains and has been ordered to stop it. Instead he reveals his own brother was ruined by the same men, and lets her pass. Emotional beat: unexpected solidarity; the cost of complicity.

chapters.title: Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. As the Corvina pulls away, Brogan's superiors arrive too late; within days the ledger reaches prosecutors and the conspiracy unravels publicly. But Hazel's reading of letters is exposed during testimony preparations, forcing her to face Edith with the truth of ten years' small betrayals. Emotional beat: victory shadowed by reckoning.

chapters.title: Juniper and the Lantern
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Edith forgives her—not because the betrayals were harmless, but because they were faithful in the ways that mattered. Hazel testifies under her own name, then takes work organizing workers' literacy circles, no longer invisible. The final image: a lantern lit in her own window. Emotional beat: belonging claimed, not granted.
